description: Bar gate stock graphs, just-in-time stock control, and managing supplier relationships.
content_html:
Why Stock Management Matters

Every business that sells physical goods must manage its stock. Too little stock and a business runs out of products, loses sales and frustrates customers. Too much stock ties up cash, takes up warehouse space and risks goods becoming damaged or obsolete. Getting the balance right is a key operational challenge for any growing business.

The three types of stock a manufacturing business might hold are: raw materials (inputs waiting to be used), work in progress (partially made goods), and finished goods (ready to sell). Service businesses have fewer physical stock concerns, but still manage consumables and equipment.

Reading Bar Gate Stock Graphs

A bar gate stock graph (also called a stock control chart) shows stock levels over time. The saw-tooth pattern is typical: stock falls steadily as goods are used or sold, then jumps back up when a new delivery arrives. Businesses use these graphs to monitor stock and trigger re-orders at the right moment.

Four key values appear on a bar gate stock graph:

  • Maximum stock level — the most stock the business wants to hold at any one time, set to avoid over-stocking.
  • Minimum stock level (buffer stock) — a safety net kept in reserve. If stock falls to this level, a re-order is urgent.
  • Re-order level — the point at which the business places a new order with its supplier. Set above the minimum to allow time for delivery.
  • Re-order quantity — the amount ordered each time, designed to bring stock back to maximum level.
Key Fact

The re-order level is set above the minimum stock level to account for lead time — the gap between placing an order and receiving delivery. If lead time is long, the re-order level must be set higher so the business does not run out before the delivery arrives.

Just-in-Time Stock Control

Just-in-time (JIT) is an approach to stock management where materials are ordered and delivered only when they are needed. The aim is to hold no unnecessary stock, cutting storage costs and reducing waste. Toyota pioneered this system in the 1970s and it has since spread across many industries.

JIT offers significant advantages for businesses with reliable suppliers and predictable demand. However, it carries real risks: if a delivery is delayed, production can grind to a halt entirely. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many manufacturers found their JIT supply chains disrupted when deliveries from overseas suppliers stopped, leading to costly production stoppages.

Advantages: Reduces storage costs because the business holds little or no stock. Frees up cash that would otherwise be tied up in unsold goods. Reduces the risk of stock becoming damaged, outdated or unsaleable. Forces businesses to build tight, reliable supplier relationships.

Disadvantages: Very sensitive to supply disruptions — one late delivery can stop production. Requires extremely reliable suppliers, which may be difficult to guarantee. Less flexibility to cope with sudden surges in demand. Businesses may miss volume-purchase discounts because they order smaller quantities more frequently.

Procurement and Supplier Relationships

Procurement is the process of sourcing and buying the inputs a business needs. Effective procurement is not just about finding the cheapest supplier — it involves evaluating quality, reliability, delivery speed and building long-term trust.

When choosing a supplier, a business weighs up several factors:

  • Quality — consistent quality from suppliers reduces defects and returns, protecting the business’s reputation.
  • Delivery cost, speed and reliability — slow or unreliable deliveries can delay production and disappoint customers.
  • Availability — can the supplier provide what is needed, in the right quantities, when required?
  • Cost — lower input costs improve profit margins, but not at the expense of quality or reliability.
  • Trust — long-term supplier relationships built on honesty and fair dealing can provide preferential terms and priority service.
Key Fact

Supplier decisions affect far more than purchase costs. A reliable, high-quality supplier can improve customer satisfaction, protect brand reputation and keep production running smoothly. A poor supplier choice can damage all three.

Logistics, Supply Chains and Business Performance

The supply chain covers every step from raw material to finished product in the hands of the customer. Good supply chain management reduces costs, ensures consistent quality and helps the business respond quickly to changes in demand. Poor supply chain decisions — such as relying on a single supplier or using slow logistics — raise costs, create delays and damage the business’s reputation.

Logistics refers to managing the physical movement of goods — transportation, warehousing and distribution. Efficient logistics reduce costs (lower transport and storage fees), protect customer satisfaction (goods arrive on time and undamaged) and free up capital that might otherwise sit in slow-moving stock.

Students sometimes assume a business should always choose the cheapest supplier. This ignores the full picture. A cheap supplier that delivers late or provides poor-quality materials may cost more in the long run through production stoppages, customer complaints and wasted inputs. Quality, reliability and trust can outweigh a small price difference, especially for businesses whose reputation depends on consistent output.
exam_tip_html: For “Outline” questions (3 marks), give two linked points in context — for example, state what JIT is and connect it to the business described in the question. For “Justify a Recommendation” (12 marks), you do not need to discuss both options equally: pick one, develop it fully with at least two analytical points tied to the case study context, acknowledge the drawback, then reach a clear justified conclusion. Answers that simply list features of both options without judgement stall in the Developing tier.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bar gate stock graphs show stock levels over time; the re-order level is set above minimum stock to account for lead time, and the gap between them is the buffer stock.
  • Just-in-time (JIT) minimises storage costs by ordering stock only when needed, but relies on reliable suppliers — any disruption can halt production entirely.
  • Good procurement weighs quality, delivery speed, reliability, availability, cost and trust; strong supplier relationships improve costs, reputation and customer satisfaction.

practice_questions.text: The bar gate stock graph for Merton Furniture Ltd shows a re-order level of 400 units and a minimum stock level of 150 units. What is the buffer stock held by the business?
practice_questions.marks: 150 units [1 mark]. The buffer stock is the minimum stock level shown on the graph.

practice_questions.text: State two factors a business should consider when choosing a supplier.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each (up to 2 marks) for any two of: quality of goods supplied / delivery cost / speed of delivery / reliability of delivery / availability of stock / cost / trust and long-term relationship. Accept any two distinct factors.

practice_questions.text: Rivington Bakery supplies artisan bread to local cafes. The owner is considering switching to a just-in-time stock system for flour and other ingredients. Outline one benefit and one drawback of just-in-time for Rivington Bakery.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Award 1 mark for identifying a benefit (e.g. reduces storage costs / frees up cash), 1 mark for developing it in context (e.g. Rivington Bakery uses small premises so less storage space needed), 1 mark for identifying a drawback with context (e.g. if a flour delivery is delayed, Rivington Bakery cannot bake and will lose sales that day). Do not award marks for bare identification without any development.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which good supplier relationships can benefit a growing business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks per point (1 for a statement, 1 for a first development, 1 for a second development). No case-study context is required for this question type.

Acceptable points include:
- Reliable delivery schedules mean a business can plan production confidently, avoiding costly stoppages. This keeps output consistent and protects customer satisfaction.
- Trusted long-term suppliers may offer preferential pricing or priority delivery, reducing input costs and improving profit margins over time.
- High-quality inputs from a dependable supplier reduce defects and returns, protecting the business’s reputation with customers.
- A supplier who communicates openly about delays allows the business to adjust its plans rather than being caught off-guard.

Mark the best two points only.

practice_questions.text: Cobble Lane Coffee is an independent café in Manchester with two locations. It orders its coffee beans weekly from a specialist roaster 200 miles away. Deliveries occasionally arrive two days late, causing the café to run out of its most popular blend. The owner is considering: Option A — switch to a local supplier with slightly lower-quality beans but guaranteed next-day delivery; or Option B — increase the minimum stock level and order fortnightly from the current roaster to build a bigger buffer. Analyse the likely impact of each option on Cobble Lane Coffee’s costs and customer satisfaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Analyses both options with specific reference to context (Manchester locations, popular blend, delivery delay pattern). Examines how each option affects both costs and customer satisfaction with developed analytical chains. Reaches a supported view about which is more effective for this business.

Secure (5–7 marks): Discusses both options with some reference to context. Makes links between the option and its effect on either costs or customer satisfaction for each, but may not fully develop both dimensions for both options.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies impacts for one or both options but with limited context application. May list features rather than analyse effects.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple points about stock management or supplier choice with little or no application to Cobble Lane Coffee’s situation.

Content guidance: Option A — costs may rise (local premium, but removes stockout losses); customer satisfaction improves (no run-outs of popular blend, but regulars may notice quality difference). Option B — higher buffer increases storage costs and ties up more cash; reduces frequency of stockouts; maintains quality but does not eliminate risk of long delays.

practice_questions.text: Kestrel Cycles is an e-bike start-up in Bristol that assembles bikes from imported components. It currently holds 30 days’ worth of components as buffer stock. The operations manager wants to introduce just-in-time stock control to cut costs. The finance director argues the business should keep its current buffer stock levels. Justify a recommendation for which approach Kestrel Cycles should adopt.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A fully developed recommendation for one option, with at least two analytical points grounded in Kestrel Cycles’ context (e-bike assembly, imported components, start-up stage). Acknowledges the strongest counter-argument and explains why the chosen option is still preferable. Conclusion adds evaluative judgement, not a summary.

Secure (7–9 marks): Clear recommendation with developed reasoning tied to context. May not fully address the counter-argument or the conclusion may partially re-state earlier points.

Developing (4–6 marks): Recommends an option but reasoning is general (not specific to Kestrel Cycles). May discuss both options in parallel without making a clear judgement.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Simple points about JIT or buffer stock with little application.

Content guidance: JIT recommendation — saves storage costs (critical for a start-up with limited capital), reduces cash tied up in stock, but relies on reliable international suppliers (risk: shipping delays could halt assembly). Buffer stock recommendation — protects against import delays (especially important for imported components with long lead times), maintains production continuity, but ties up cash and increases storage costs at a stage when cash flow is tight.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the 're-order level' on a bar gate stock graph indicate?
options: The maximum amount of stock the business should ever hold
The point at which a new order is placed with the supplier
The amount of stock destroyed due to damage
The quantity of stock sold to customers each week

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a key disadvantage of just-in-time stock control?
options: It always results in higher storage costs
It forces businesses to overstock raw materials
A single delivery delay can halt production entirely
It requires businesses to employ more warehouse staff

knowledge_checks.q: The gap between placing an order with a supplier and receiving the delivery is called the _____.
_____ is a stock management method where materials arrive only as they are needed in production, holding virtually no buffer stock.
Match each stock control term to its correct meaning:
right: The minimum stock held as a safety reserve
The stock level at which a new order is triggered
The time between ordering and receiving stock

flashcard_questions.q: What is a bar gate stock graph?
flashcard_questions.a: A graph showing stock levels over time with a saw-tooth pattern as stock is used and replenished.
The minimum stock level kept as a safety reserve in case deliveries are delayed.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'lead time' mean in stock management?
flashcard_questions.a: The time between placing an order and receiving the delivery from the supplier.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must the re-order level be set above the minimum stock level?
flashcard_questions.a: To allow time for the delivery to arrive before stock runs out.
Ordering materials only when needed in production, holding little or no buffer stock.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one financial advantage of just-in-time for a business.
flashcard_questions.a: It reduces storage costs and frees up cash tied up in unsold stock.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one risk of using just-in-time stock control.
flashcard_questions.a: A single delivery delay can stop production entirely.
The process of finding, agreeing terms with, and obtaining goods from suppliers.

flashcard_questions.q: Apart from price, name one factor a business considers when choosing a supplier.
flashcard_questions.a: Reliability of delivery (also accept: quality / speed / availability / trust).

flashcard_questions.q: How does a reliable supplier protect a business’s reputation?
flashcard_questions.a: Consistent quality inputs reduce defects and returns, keeping customers satisfied.
The network from raw material to end customer, including suppliers, manufacturers and distributors.

flashcard_questions.q: Which company pioneered just-in-time stock control in the 1970s?
flashcard_questions.a: Toyota — the Japanese car manufacturer that developed JIT as part of its lean production system.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a business choose a slightly more expensive but reliable supplier over a cheaper one?
flashcard_questions.a: Unreliable supply can cause costly production stoppages and damage customer satisfaction.

glossary_terms.definition: The raw materials, components and finished products a business holds, ready for use or sale.
A graph showing how stock levels change over time, with a saw-tooth pattern as stock is used and replenished.
A stock management system where materials and components arrive only as they are needed in production, holding virtually no buffer stock.
The process of finding, agreeing terms with, and obtaining goods and services from suppliers.
The network of suppliers, manufacturers, distributors and retailers involved in getting a product from raw material to end customer.
The management of the flow of goods, information and other resources between the point of origin and the point of consumption.
